title: Classic Bloom filter
description: A Bloom filter answers 'definitely not in the set, or probably in the set' using a bit array and k hash functions: insert sets k bits, query checks all k. No false negatives ever; false positives tunable by size. A 1% false-positive filter needs ~10 bits per element — ten times smaller than storing the keys. It is the standard 'check cheaply before the expensive lookup' structure.
mechanism: m-bit array, k hashes. Add: set bits h1..hk. Query: all k bits set -> maybe present. Optimal k = (m/n) ln 2 for n elements.
algo: O(k) per op. False positive rate = (1 - e^(-kn/m))^k; optimal ~0.6185^(m/n).

title: False positive math
description: The false-positive rate is not magic — it is (1 - e^(-kn/m))^k, minimized at k = (m/n) ln 2 to about 0.6185^(m/n). Ten bits per element gives ~1%, twenty gives ~0.01%. This formula sizes every Bloom filter in production: pick your acceptable FP rate, solve for m/n, set k. More hashes past the optimum actually hurt.
mechanism: Derive from the probability a bit stays 0 after kn insertions: (1-1/m)^(kn) ~= e^(-kn/m). A query hits k bits; all set with probability (1 - e^(-kn/m))^k.
algo: Closed form — compute, don't guess. Diminishing returns past ~20 bits/element.
demo:
import math

def fp_rate(m_over_n, k=None):
    k = k or m_over_n * math.log(2)
    return (1 - math.exp(-k / m_over_n)) ** k

print('bits/elem : false-positive rate (optimal k)')
for b in (4, 8, 10, 16, 20):
    print('%9d : %.4f%%' % (b, fp_rate(b) * 100))
print('rule of thumb: 10 bits/element ~= 1%% FP; double bits -> square the error')

title: Optimal hash count
description: The optimal number of hash functions is k = (m/n) ln 2 — about 7 for the classic 10-bits-per-element filter. Fewer hashes underuse the bits; more hashes set too many bits and raise the FP rate. In practice, two real hashes generate k via double hashing (h1 + i*h2), so 'k hashes' costs two hash computations, not k.
mechanism: k_opt minimizes (1-e^(-kn/m))^k. Double hashing: position_i = (h1 + i*h2 + i^2) mod m gives k well-distributed positions from 2 hashes (Kirsch-Mitzenmacher).
algo: O(2) hash computations + O(k) modular arithmetic per op.
demo:
import hashlib, math

def h1h2(key):
    d = hashlib.md5(key.encode()).digest()
    return int.from_bytes(d[:8], 'big'), int.from_bytes(d[8:], 'big')

m, n = 1000, 100
k = round(m / n * math.log(2))
h1, h2 = h1h2('vector')
positions = [(h1 + i * h2) % m for i in range(k)]  # k positions from 2 hashes
print('optimal k for m/n=10: %d' % k)
print('positions from double hashing:', positions)
print('2 hash computations, %d bit positions: Kirsch-Mitzenmacher' % k)

title: Counting Bloom filter
description: Classic Bloom filters cannot delete — clearing bits might erase other elements' fingerprints. Counting Bloom filters replace bits with small counters: insert increments k counters, delete decrements, query checks all k > 0. Counters are 3-4 bits each (overflow is rare and only raises FP slightly). They suit dynamic sets like cache admission lists and flow tables.
mechanism: Array of c-bit counters. Add: increment k counters (saturating). Remove: decrement. Query: all k counters nonzero. Size ~c*x bits vs 1 bit for classic.
algo: O(k) per op, 3-4x the memory of classic. Counter overflow probability negligible at 4 bits for normal loads.

title: Scalable Bloom filter
description: A Bloom filter sized for n elements degrades as the set grows past n — the FP rate climbs. Scalable Bloom filters chain a series of filters with geometrically growing sizes and tightening FP rates: when one fills, a bigger one is added. Queries check all filters; the compound FP rate stays bounded. They fit unbounded streams where n is unknown upfront.
mechanism: Filter i has size m*r^i and FP rate p*s^i (r~2, s~0.9). Insert into the newest non-full filter. Query: check newest first, then older. Total FP <= p/(1-s).
algo: O(filters * k) query; filters grow logarithmically with n. Memory within a constant factor of a perfectly-sized filter.

title: Cuckoo filter
description: Cuckoo filters store short fingerprints in a cuckoo hash table: lookup checks two buckets for the fingerprint, insert kicks occupants to their alternate bucket like a cuckoo chick. They support deletion (remove the fingerprint), use less space than Bloom at low FP rates, and lookups touch at most 2 cache lines. The trade is a load-factor ceiling (~95%) and occasional rebuilds on insert failure.
mechanism: fingerprint = short hash of key; bucket1 = h(key), bucket2 = bucket1 XOR h(fingerprint). Lookup: fingerprint in either bucket. Insert: place or displace (bounded kicks); failure -> rebuild bigger.
algo: O(1) lookup (2 buckets). Insert amortized O(1); ~95% max load. Deletion is safe — no false negatives introduced.

title: Quotient filter
description: Quotient filters store fingerprints in a compact hash table with linear probing metadata (is-occupied/is-continuation/is-shifted bits), giving Bloom-like space with exact counting, deletion, and merging. They are cache-friendly (one cache line per query typically) and support resizing. The design is more intricate than Bloom, but the feature set — delete, merge, enumerate — wins for dynamic compact sets.
mechanism: Split hash into quotient q (bucket) and remainder r (stored). Three metadata bits per slot resolve collisions and enable shifting. Query reconstructs the canonical slot from the metadata runs.
algo: O(1) expected ops, one cache line typical. Space ~2-3 bits overhead per element over the fingerprint size.

title: XOR filter
description: XOR filters are the speed champions: ~1.23x the space of a perfect hash table, 3 memory accesses per lookup, and construction in linear time. They store fingerprints such that key's fingerprint = XOR of 3 table positions; lookup recomputes the XOR and compares. Immutable after build (like Bloom), but faster queries and less space — the modern default for static sets.
mechanism: Build: map each key to 3 positions via a peeling process on a 3-uniform hypergraph; store fingerprints so XOR(positions) = fingerprint(key). Query: compute positions, XOR stored values, compare to fingerprint(key).
algo: O(1) query, 3 accesses. Build O(n) expected. ~9 bits/element at 1% FP — beats Bloom.
demo:
# XOR filter idea: fingerprint(key) == T[h1] XOR T[h2] XOR T[h3].
import hashlib
N = 64
T = [0] * N
keys = ['alpha', 'beta', 'gamma']

def fp(k):
    return int(hashlib.md5(('f' + k).encode()).hexdigest(), 16) & 0xFF

def hs(k):
    d = hashlib.md5(('h' + k).encode()).hexdigest()
    return [int(d[i:i+8], 16) % N for i in (0, 8, 16)]

# toy build: store fingerprint at h1 (real build solves the 3-XOR system)
for k in keys:
    T[hs(k)[0]] ^= fp(k)

def contains(k):
    h1, h2, h3 = hs(k)
    return (T[h1] ^ T[h2] ^ T[h3]) == fp(k)

print('alpha:', contains('alpha'), '| missing "zzz":', contains('zzz'))
print('real XOR filters solve all 3 positions (peeling); lookups = 3 accesses')

title: Ribbon filter
description: Ribbon filters push space even lower (~1% over optimal) with a banded linear-system construction that is fast to build and friendly to modern CPUs. They generalize: the same structure supports counting and homomorphic operations. RocksDB adopted Ribbon as an alternative to Bloom for SSTable filters — same API, less memory, comparable speed.
mechanism: Solve a banded linear system over GF(2): each key constrains a short band of the table; Gaussian elimination on bands is O(n * width). Query reads the band and checks the equation.
algo: Build O(n*w) for band width w (~64); query O(w). Space within ~1% of the information-theoretic lower bound.
demo:
# Ribbon in one picture: each key's fingerprint is a linear equation over a short
# band of the table. Query = evaluate the band. Space ~= optimal.
import hashlib
W, N = 8, 64
T = [0] * N

def band(key):
    h = int(hashlib.md5(key.encode()).hexdigest(), 16)
    start = h % (N - W)
    return start, [(h >> (i * 3)) & 0xFF for i in range(W)]

# toy: store fingerprint xored across its band
def fp(k):
    return int(hashlib.md5(('r' + k).encode()).hexdigest(), 16) & 0xFF

for k in ['k1', 'k2']:
    s, coeffs = band(k)
    T[s] ^= fp(k)  # (real Ribbon solves the banded system properly)

s, _ = band('k1')
print('band start for k1:', s, '| stored value nonzero:', T[s] != 0)
print('real Ribbon: banded Gaussian elimination, ~1%% over optimal space')

title: Bloom filters in LSM-trees
description: LSM-trees keep a Bloom filter per SSTable: a point lookup checks each level's filter and skips SSTables that definitely lack the key. With 10 bits/key and a 1% FP rate, a 7-level lookup touches ~1 SSTable instead of 7 — the difference between fast and unusable. This single optimization is why LSM point lookups compete with B-trees.
mechanism: On SSTable flush, build a filter over its keys. Point lookup: for each level, newest SSTable first, check filter; only open SSTables whose filter says 'maybe'. Filters live in memory (block cache).
algo: Without filters: O(levels) SSTable opens. With: O(1 + levels * FP_rate) expected — ~1 open at 1% FP.

title: Blocked Bloom filters
description: Blocked Bloom filters split the bit array into cache-line-sized blocks (512 bits) and hash each key into a single block — one cache miss per query instead of k scattered ones. They trade a slightly higher FP rate for dramatically better locality. CPU caches love them: a lookup touches one 64-byte line, and SIMD sets/tests all k bits at once.
mechanism: First hash picks the block; remaining hashes pick bits within the block. Insert/query confined to one block. SIMD kernels process the block's bits in parallel.
algo: O(1) cache miss per query vs O(k) for classic. Slightly higher FP at the same bits/element — usually worth it.

title: Choosing k and m in practice
description: Textbook sizing assumes uniform hashes and known n — production adds margins: size for 1.5x expected n (growth), round k to the nearest integer, and measure the real FP rate on your keys (adversarial or correlated keys break the math). If n is truly unknown, use a scalable filter. If deletions are needed, use counting/Cuckoo. The formula starts the design; the workload finishes it.
mechanism: m = -n ln(p) / (ln 2)^2 for target FP p; k = (m/n) ln 2. Add growth headroom. Validate empirically: insert real keys, query real non-keys, measure.
algo: Closed-form sizing + empirical validation. Revisit when the key distribution shifts.
demo:
import math

def size_for(n, p):
    m = -n * math.log(p) / (math.log(2) ** 2)
    k = (m / n) * math.log(2)
    return m, k

n = 1_000_000
for p in (0.01, 0.001):
    m, k = size_for(n * 1.5, p)  # 1.5x headroom for growth
    print('target FP %.3f: m=%.0f bits (%.1f MB), k=%.1f -> use k=%d' %
          (p, m, m / 8 / 1e6, k, round(k)))
print('then measure real FP on YOUR keys: correlated keys break the formula')

title: Alternatives to Bloom
description: Bloom filters are not always the answer: exact structures (hash sets) win when memory is plentiful and zero FP is required; Cuckoo/XOR filters win for static sets; quotient filters win when deletion and merging matter; and sometimes the best filter is no filter (tiny SSTables are cheaper to just open). Choose by the constraint that binds: memory, FP tolerance, mutability, or speed.
mechanism: Decision inputs: static vs dynamic set, acceptable FP rate, memory budget, query latency SLO. Static + low FP -> XOR; dynamic + delete -> Cuckoo/counting; merge needed -> quotient; zero FP -> hash set.
algo: A decision table, not an algorithm — but it saves more memory than any single structure choice.

title: Bloom filter serialization
description: Filters must survive restarts: SSTable filters are serialized alongside the data and memory-mapped on open. The format is just the bit array plus (m, k, hash seed) — a few bytes of header. Version the format; a filter built with a different hash seed is garbage. Lazy loading (read the filter only when the SSTable is first queried) keeps restarts fast.
mechanism: Header: magic, version, m, k, seed. Body: bit array. On open: mmap the region, verify magic/version, wrap without copying. Checksums guard against torn writes.
algo: O(m) to write once; O(1) to map on open. Lazy load defers even the mapping.

title: Measuring real FP rates
description: The formula predicts; production measures. Real FP rates diverge from theory when keys are correlated (sequential ids share hash prefixes in weak hashes), when n was underestimated, or when the hash function is poor. The measurement harness inserts the real key set, queries a held-out non-key set, and reports the empirical rate — then sizes up or switches hashes if it misses the target.
mechanism: Split keys into inserted and held-out sets; build the filter on inserted; query held-out; FP = positives / held_out. Repeat across time windows to catch distribution drift.
algo: O(n + held_out) measurement. Run in CI on representative key samples.
